name: Treaty at Camp Lu-pi-yu-ma, on the south side of Clear Lake (1851), unratified California treaty O
aka: Treaty O of the eighteen unratified California treaties of 1851-1852
citation: Never ratified; printed by order of the Senate, January 19, 1905
promises: Article 4 set apart as a reservation, its use 'forever guaranteed' to the tribes and to other tribes the United States might move there, the part of the Clear Lake valley west of Mount McKee, the habitable part estimated at about twelve miles by six, with the exclusive right of fishing in that part of the lake.
Article 5: one hundred head of beef cattle and two hundred fifty-pound sacks of flour in 1851, and the same in each of 1852 and 1853.
Article 6: clothing, cloth, blankets, iron and steel in each of the two years after ratification, and in the first year brood mares, milch cows, work cattle, wagons, mules, ploughs, seed and tools.

Article 7: a farmer with two assistants, a carpenter, a blacksmith, a principal school teacher with two male and two female assistant teachers, paid by the United States for five years and as long after as the President thought advisable.

breaches.what: This treaty (treaty O in the President's schedule) was one of eighteen made with California Indians in 1851-52 that the Senate refused to ratify in executive session on July 8, 1852, and placed under an injunction of secrecy that was removed only on January 18, 1905.

breaches.what: Congress let the Indians of California sue for lands the United States took without compensation, and declared their loss from failing to secure the lands and compensation in the eighteen unratified treaties sufficient ground for equitable relief.

breaches.what: The Big Valley Band of Pomo Indians states that the 1851 treaty reserving about 72 square miles on the south side of Clear Lake for its ancestors was refused ratification and sealed, and that without a treaty or a filed land claim its ancestors were left landless.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Big Valley Band of Pomo Indians, About Us page of its tribal website

source.title: About Us
source.publisher: Big Valley Band of Pomo Indians

landTaken: The tribes' lands in California, taken without the reserved tract or compensation; Royce areas 295, 296 mark the cession and the intended reservation.
compensation: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 the Court of Claims could award the value of the lands and compensation proposed in the eighteen treaties, with land at $1.25 an acre, less offsets. The amount finally paid was not located in this pass.
today: The treaty remains unratified. The National Archives' 2013 account describes the rejection as leaving most California Indians without land.

nationVoice.nation: Big Valley Band of Pomo Indians
nationVoice.summary: The Band, descendants of the Xa-Ben-Na-Po Band of Pomo, says its leaders agreed in 1851 to a treaty setting aside about 72 square miles on the south side of Clear Lake including Mt. Konocti, that the Senate refused to ratify it on July 8, 1852 and sealed it until 1905, and that, unaware of the land claims deadline, its ancestors became landless; the seven Lake County Pomo tribes now hold under half a percent of the county.

openQuestions: The Senate never ratified this treaty, so its promises never bound the United States; it is shown as never ratified. The 1928 Act is recorded as the government's own acknowledgment of the loss.
One record covers the whole set of eighteen treaties for the facts common to all; the other seventeen are the cession-1851-* and cession-1852-* entries for Royce areas 273 to 310.

The tribal names are as the commissioners wrote them in 1851-52; most are village or local group names, not nations, and how each community names itself today was not established. treaties.json lists as present-day tribes: Big Valley Band of Pomo Indians of the Big Valley Rancheria, California; Middletown Rancheria of Pomo Indians of California; Robinson Rancheria of Pomo Indians of California.

The Court of Claims judgment under the 1928 Act (Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583, 1942) and the Indian Claims Commission settlement for the Indians of California (Dockets 31 and 37) were not opened in this pass; they are the leads for the amounts paid.

In Article 3 the signing tribes gave up their claims to other lands; because the Senate rejected the treaty, the United States took the land without the reserved tract or the promised goods (1928 Act, section 2).
Audit 2026-11-08: promises corrected against treaty O as printed in Heizer (1972), the treaty text at https://digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu/record/83366/files/arfs003-001.pdf.
